On Morocco, Russia, and Western Sahara: 

Russia no longer has the strategic foothold in Syria that it once enjoyed, its old friend Gaddafi is long gone, and the fallout from Wagner has complicated Moscow's ability to pursue a coherent strategy across Africa. So yes, of course that keeping the Western Sahara conflict alive serves a larger Russian objective of obstructing U.S. influence and preventing the emergence of stronger regional partnerships that could challenge Moscow's interests.

More importantly, the Russians have also failed to appreciate how much Morocco's position has changed. The kingdom isn't simply an American ally in North Africa anymore. Morocco has become a major economic and financial power in West Africa, with Moroccan banks controlling nearly 30% of the West African banking market, and Moroccan investments spanning telecommunications, fertilizers, infrastructure, and industry. The proposed $25 billion Nigeria-Morocco Atlantic Gas Pipeline, stretching approximately 6,900 kilometers across 13 countries, could further transform the kingdom's strategic importance by connecting West African energy markets to Europe, which will inevitably make Russian gas irrelevant. 

It's safe to say that Moscow has certainly noticed this transformation, which explains why Russian diplomatic rhetoric has become increasingly accommodating toward Rabat (as I pointed out in their draft). But the underlying calculation hasn't changed since Russia still treats an abstention, rather than a favorable vote, as a diplomatic concession for which Morocco should offer something in return. That approach may have worked when Moscow enjoyed greater leverage, but Morocco's growing strategic weight has fundamentally changed the equation.

By vetoing today's resolution, Moscow apparently believed it could reaffirm its commitment to Algeria, one of its principal regional partners, while preserving its ability to bargain with Morocco. But the Russians have misread the room. Rabat now has much less reason to believe that engagement with Moscow produces meaningful diplomatic returns.

In many ways, this could be a blessing in disguise for Morocco, exposing Russia's priorities and giving Rabat every reason to deepen its alignment with Washington and Europe. Putin is accelerating the very Western alignment he wanted prevent.

tweets.text:
#Uranium producers need contracts that make mines worth building.

A margin over reported cash costs is NOT the same as an adequate return on the full investment.

Exploration. Permitting. Mine construction. Processing infrastructure. Labour and energy. Sustaining capital. Financing. Closure.

Plus a return that justifies years of capital at risk.

Headline production costs capture only part of that equation. Producers should demand contract prices and terms that support the entire investment.

For investors, scale matters. Smaller standalone mines can carry substantial infrastructure, regulatory and corporate costs spread across relatively few pounds. Those burdens do not shrink neatly with the deposit.

Larger operations with long mine lives can spread investment and fixed costs across more production.

My preference: scale, longevity and margins that can survive a difficult cycle.

Size alone guarantees nothing. Grade, recovery, mining method and existing infrastructure can make smaller projects competitive. But a small mine with a large funding requirement deserves serious scrutiny.

The price that keeps an existing mine running is not necessarily the price that gets the next one built. New mines need uranium >$200 (at least most mines, a few tier-1 mines might do with a bit less). That is now. Inflation-adjusted it will be much more when the mine is built in 10-20 years.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text: I am getting even more convinced that #uranium prices must hit a minimum of $200 to incentivize enough new supply. The increase in production costs is huge all over the world. $CCJ

The US tokenization exemption is exciting but for the foreseeable future it's not going to be where the action is. As Eleanor's note makes clear, it's going to be roadblock after roadblock.

Disruptive technologies always start on the edges, serving people who are poorly served by the existing system. For stocks, that means the 4+ billion people who don't have access to US stocks, crypto-native investors who are used to 24/7/365 trading, and active traders who want to execute strategies the existing system doesn't support. Those are very big markets.

TradFi overestimates TradFi tokenization and underestimates degen tokenization.

Chamath: The AI Boom Has a Borrowing Problem

“The entire United States economy is levered to the AI complex.

So very narrowly, we're talking about seven or eight companies that set the tone for the entire country. And whether we like it or not, that is where we are.

Why do I say that? The most important companies in the world are in a massive spending binge, right?

These were highly profitable, highly cash accretive, highly cash flow generative businesses that have said, ‘We're going to put the foot down on spending because we believe in what's coming into the future.’ That's what drives GDP and it's what drives growth.

Now, as they do that though, they deplete their cash and they have to raise debt.

The AI complex now owes $340-400 billion to the market. And you'd say, ‘Okay, why is that important?’

The problem is this: These companies are raising so much money it starts to crowd out the capital markets.

And the most important part of the capital market that it starts to crowd out, is the appetite for government treasuries.

And what you can see here is that when you look at these AI firms, the amount of money that they need to raise through the end of '27, it's 30% of all of what the Treasury's about to issue in that same period.

So, whether we like it or not, they are going to start competing for demand.”

You’ve read the election think pieces...by the same people who have been spanked hard by every cycle since Trump upset over Hilary. 

You’ve refreshed the Polymarket dashboard….the same dashboard that had no predictive value in the Brazilian election.  

You’ve looked closely at the economic data….despite being well aware that the economy is increasingly K-shaped with wide divergences between regions and sectors.  

You know that Dems cluster in certain professions and have very different income vs asset characteristics vs independents and repubs but that seems to be overly nuanced for you so you just move on.  

You have loudly proclaimed Trump has no morals or values and yet are utterly confused by his actions that seem to be antithetical to winning elections which seems bizarre to you for someone who went through a series of harrying persecutions and raids which will surely reoccur if Dems are back in power.  

You just shrug and assure yourself you are smart enough and diligent enough to catch inconsistencies when you read the think pieces and therefore are utterly certain republicans have no shot at winning the house.  

Instead take five minutes and try to understand what real wage growth looks like for the median voter.  

The independent in swing states.  

What drives voter turnout historically and how animated the respective bases are.  

What the polling error was historically but more importantly what caused those errors to worsen and is that deterioration in methodology accelerating or decelerating.  

Spend two seconds clicking down to the individual house race level and looking at the top gamblers in each race.  

How large are the pools.  How much are they betting.  What is their track.  What other races are they betting on.  

If you did this as I have you will see it’s the blind leading the blind.  

There is clearly a systematic spend dynamic happening where someone is just sprinkling bets across races based on polling at the individual race level without differentiated data or methodology.   

You think you can predict the future.  

And yet you barely understand the admin or Washington or what has motivated voters historically.  

When the republicans sweep I hope people use this as a learning opportunity and understand how utterly psyoped they are by the mid-IQ pundit class.  

These people should be sent to the gulag and re-trained as plumbers.  They should not be pontificating in the FT or on CNN. 

🫡
